title: Leg Day + Bulk Update (Hypertrophy Log #2)
summary: Second Hypertrophy Log showing two lower-body days: one opening with heavy RDLs then Bulgarian split squats and calves, the other with pause SSB squats supersetted with a serratus/rib rehab move and neck, then single-leg RDLs, calves and front neck. NH explains his lower-day structure inside an upper/lower everyday split and gives a bulk update: about 210 to 215 lb since November, aiming for a very slow multi-year bulk driven by gym performance.
claims: Leg days reveal whether someone is a serious lifter; many people skip or half-ass them
Leg days should have roughly 60-70% of the exercises of upper days; he does 4-5 lower exercises versus 6-8 upper
He never stretches or does mobility work before lifting; he warms up with 4-5 lighter sets of the lift, adding 50 lb per set up to the top set
Every lower day opens with a heavy knee flexion or a heavy hip hinge, which dictates the rest of the day, taken to RIR 0-1
He often takes RDLs to failure because they are very safe for his build; he pauses and breathes before the last rep
Do 2-4 sets of RDLs depending on how you feel; if you hit the top of the rep range add sets, and next week go up in weight with fewer sets to match the stimulus
The first heavy lower exercise is not put in a giant set, though it can be supersetted with small muscles like neck, abs, curls or rear delts that don't compromise bracing
If a lower day opens with a hip hinge, the next heavy movement is a knee flexion, and vice versa
If an exercise in your lower body routine isn't hard, it's probably not giving results; do not dodge difficulty
Use straps on Bulgarian split squats; grip should never limit a leg exercise
On Bulgarian split squats keep the front foot straight to limit external hip rotation and glute/hamstring involvement
Double progression: repeat a weight until you hit the top of the rep range (12), then increase
Training calves right after quads in a giant set does not hurt performance
On calf raises never let the heel touch the floor, pause at the bottom and keep a slow tempo so you do not rebound off the Achilles tendon
He neglected calves for years; at 17+ inches they look puny next to his big upper legs, so train them hard
Lower days with only 3 exercises are more strenuous than his 7-exercise upper days
On pause squats the negative tempo should never change; the only sign of approaching failure is the positive slowing to a crawl
The SSB keeps the weight over midfoot so you can safely push pause squats close to failure
He broke ribs on both sides doing squats and has done a banded rotational serratus punch rehab exercise for three years
Band neck extensions driven by a hip hinge with the head resisting feel more natural and safer than lying with a plate on the head
Neck is almost never limiting, so supersetting neck training is easy; no excuses
Never do more than two giant-set lines or five exercises on a leg day; usually four
Single-leg RDLs are his favorite hamstring exercise: they barely tax the lower back, work hip external rotation and are rehab-friendly
Do single-leg RDLs to torso parallel, holding something for balance or with a band around your waist anchored to a rack
On leg day compounds are 80-90% of the work; isolation is secondary
Calves need frequent, hard training; he trains them every leg day
Dumbbell calf raises with the dumbbell on top of the knee and pushing on it with the hands during the negative add tension
Calf training is only boring if you don't push it hard; train to a burning pump and you'll start to enjoy it
Train the front of the neck across a bench with the head floating and a slow tempo; front neck matters for facial aesthetics
Training legs 3x/week, every 48 hours, with 6-8 hard sets per day gives 18-24 lower-body sets per week, plenty for growth
He prefers intensity over volume: fewer quality sets, made possible by high frequency
He runs an everyday split built on an upper/lower template; lower days include traps, neck or abs but never big upper muscles
The more advanced you are, the slower the bulk should be; gaining 10 lb of lean mass in 2-3 months at 200 lb is physiologically impossible
The goal of a bulk is a surplus that drives gym performance and progression, not scale weight
He gained 5 lb since November with little fat, still visible abs and veins; he dislikes the fluffy state
Plan: keep bulking for maybe three years at 0.5-1 lb per month, about 10 lb per year, with no target weight
In the past, chasing 225-230 lb just made him fat because he focused on the scale over performance
